guide.title: Sea Gate, Brooklyn: A Private Enclave Behind the Gate
guide.intro: Sea Gate occupies the ground once known as Norton's Point, after the owner of a casino there, and it carried a reputation for gambling before anyone built houses on it. Alrick Man began developing it as a private residential enclave in 1892, and by 1899 the property owners included the Morgan, Dodge and Vanderbilt families. The Atlantic Yacht Club's clubhouse here, designed by Stanford White and frequented by Governor Al Smith, burned down in 1933. The community became majority Jewish by the 1930s; before that, signs in it read "no dogs or Jews." Isaac Bashevis Singer rented a room here in 1935 for four dollars a week, and the Yiddish poet Aliza Greenblatt wrote "In Sea Gate by the Sea."

sections.heading: What is behind the gate
sections.body:
Sea Gate is a private gated community of roughly 850 single-family homes. The Sea Gate Association governs it and controls access for non-residents. The main vehicle entrance is a gate on Surf Avenue, flanked by a police station and the association's office. Residents pay for their own sewer, beach, lifeguard, street-light and street-cleaning services, and for private security through the Sea Gate Public Safety Department; the NYPD's 60th Precinct patrols the area. The community was 99 percent white in 1960 and 83 percent white by the 2010 census.

The two sites described below both stand inside those gates. The Coney Island Light sits on Coast Guard property at the western tip of the peninsula, and the chapel is the first structure a visitor sees on entering the main security gate.

As of 2005 coverage, the population was largely Russian, Hasidic and elderly, with five shtibelach and a Chabad yeshiva, Tiferes Menachem. Hurricane Sandy flooded homes here in 2012, battered the shoreline and destroyed the sea wall at the neighborhood's Lindy Park.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
There is no subway station in Sea Gate. The nearest is Coney Island–Stillwell Avenue, in Coney Island, served by the D, F, N and Q.

Buses are the recorded way in. The B74 is a loop route: it begins at the Mermaid Avenue bus loop by Coney Island–Stillwell Avenue station, runs west along Mermaid Avenue to West 37th Street and into Sea Gate, terminates at West 37th Street and Neptune Avenue inside the gated community, then loops back by way of Bayview Avenue and West 33rd Street. It is the successor to the Norton's Point streetcar line, whose streetcars were replaced by motorbuses on November 7, 1948.

The X28 express bus runs between Lower Manhattan, at Thomas and Church Streets, and Bensonhurst, with a Sea Gate terminus at West 37th Street and Surf Avenue served part-time in the peak direction and on late nights only.

faq.question: How do I get to Sea Gate?
faq.answer: By B74 bus, which runs from the Mermaid Avenue bus loop at Coney Island–Stillwell Avenue station west along Mermaid Avenue and into Sea Gate, terminating at West 37th Street and Neptune Avenue. The X28 express bus from Lower Manhattan has a Sea Gate terminus at West 37th Street and Surf Avenue, served part-time in the peak direction and late nights. There is no subway station in Sea Gate; the nearest is Coney Island–Stillwell Avenue, in Coney Island.

faq.question: Can visitors go into Sea Gate?
faq.answer: Sea Gate is a private gated community. The Sea Gate Association governs it and controls access for non-residents, through a main vehicle gate on Surf Avenue flanked by a police station and the association's office. Both the lighthouse and the chapel described on this page stand inside those gates, and the lighthouse itself is on Coast Guard property.

faq.question: Can I visit the Atlantic Yacht Club clubhouse?
faq.answer: No. The Stanford White clubhouse that Governor Al Smith frequented burned down in 1933 and no longer exists.

places.name: Coney Island Light
places.address: Western tip of the Coney Island peninsula, on Coast Guard property inside Sea Gate, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: An active United States Coast Guard aid to navigation, a 75-foot steel skeletal tower also known as Norton Point Light. It stands on Coast Guard property inside Sea Gate's gated grounds.
places.history: The light was established in 1890, the present tower first lit in 1920, and the station automated by the Coast Guard in 1989. Frank Schubert kept it from 1960 until his death in 2003 and is widely described as the last civilian lighthouse keeper in the United States.

places.name: Sea Gate Chapel
places.summary: A chapel built in 1901 with stained-glass windows, described as the first structure seen on entering Sea Gate's main security gate. It stands inside the gated community.

entries.name: Coney Island Light
entries.note: The steel tower at the western tip of the peninsula, established 1890 and automated in 1989.

entries.name: Sea Gate Chapel
entries.note: A 1901 chapel just inside the main security gate.

links.note: The B74 runs from the Mermaid Avenue bus loop at Coney Island–Stillwell Avenue station west along Mermaid Avenue into Sea Gate.
The B36's two terminals are Sea Gate and Sheepshead Bay, where it ends at Gravesend Neck Road and Nostrand Avenue.
The X28 express bus serves Bensonhurst and terminates at West 37th Street and Surf Avenue in Sea Gate.
